desc:
The figure shown is an example of evaluator prompts used for MBPP+ evaluation under two conditions: with and without chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. It contains structured text blocks labeled “Evaluator prompt” — specifically Table 7 (“no reasoning”) appears before the image, while Table 8 (“with CoT”) corresponds to this figure’s content. The visible components include instruction templates for evaluating code solutions using LLMs as judges: one version asks direct yes/no judgments on correctness; another requires step-by-step verification followed by a final verdict (Correct/Incorrect). Both versions specify input format (`<code>`), output expectations, and scoring rules — including partial credit logic in the CoT variant. The structure reflects how different prompting strategies influence evaluator behavior during automated code assessment tasks.

My final verdict is $$B$$

This figure consists of four groups of bar charts comparing performance metrics for EM filtering on datasets named SIFT (EM), UQ-V (EM), Audio (EM), and Paper (EM). Each group contains three vertical axis plots: Index Construction Time, Peak Memory Usage during construction or query execution, and final index size. The methods being compared across the horizontal axes include FDANN with different filter types like "sifted" vs "filtered", CAPS variants such as "kmeans" versus raw data processing using NHQ Kgraph algorithms along side UNG baselines without any filtering applied at all . Trends show that while some approaches achieve faster indexing times they often require more memory or result in larger indices compared to others; similarly there are trade-offs between speed and resource usage depending upon which algorithm is chosen.

This figure consists of four line charts arranged side by side, each showing Recall@10 versus Queries per Second (QPS) for different query selectivity levels: 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, and 0.8 — all under EM filtering on the arxiv-for-fanns-medium dataset. Each chart plots multiple algorithms including ACORN (lower/upper bound), CAPS (kmeans/kgraph/stitched variants), FDANN (filtered/stitched/NHQ/nsw/LNG versions). The x-axis is logarithmic, ranging from 10² to over 10⁴ QPS; the y-axis ranges linearly from 0.0 to 1.0 Recall@10. Across all four charts, higher selectivity correlates with lower recall at high query rates — for example, in Selectivity = 0.8, most methods drop sharply beyond ~5×10³ QPS compared to the more stable performance seen at Selectivity = 0.2. The legend is repeated identically across each subplot and lists nine distinct algorithm configurations using color-coded markers (e.g., purple crosses for ACORN lower bound, green squares for NHQ kgraph).

This figure consists of two vertical bar charts side by side: “Llama3-8B” on the left and “GPT-4” on the right. Each chart shows four blue bars labeled 1 through 4 along the x-axis (“Average Rewrite Number”), with percentages (0% to 55%) shown as y-values for each bar height — representing how often that rewrite count occurred during adaptive selection. For Llama3-8B, most queries were rewritten twice or three times (~49–50%), while very few used only one or four rewrites (<2%). GPT-4’s distribution peaks at 1x and especially 3x rewrites (up to ~51%), with minimal use of single or quadruple rewrites. Both charts show an average rewrite number near 2.48–2.46, indicating the system typically selects around two-to-three rewrites per query under adaptive selection — far fewer than a fixed four-rewrite baseline would suggest.

This figure consists of two pie charts showing how different language models are evaluated when using Gemma-2 variants as evaluators — specifically, Figure 10 for “Gemma-2-9b-it” and the lower chart (labeled similarly) for “gemma-2-27b-it”. Each slice represents a model being evaluated, with its name and percentage of total instances shown; examples include ‘claude-3-opus’, ‘llama-3.1-flash-api’, ‘qwen-turbo-latest-v0.5’, and others like ‘gpt-4o-mini’ or ‘mistral-large’. The top chart totals 2873 evaluated instances, while the bottom one shows 3329 — both dominated by large slices from models such as Claude Opus series (around 6% each), Llama Flash API variants (~5–6%), and Qwen Turbo Latest V0.5 (~4%). Smaller segments represent less frequently selected evaluators like ‘command-r’, ‘yi-large-chat’, or ‘deepseek-coder-v2’. The structure reveals that even when using Gemma-2 models as judges, they still heavily favor other high-performing commercial systems rather than themselves — suggesting evaluator bias toward known strong performers.

This figure consists of five line charts arranged horizontally side by side under an “EM” label at top right (likely indicating EM filtering). Each chart plots Recall@k on the vertical axis against Queries Per Second (QPS) — shown as 10^2, 10^3, etc. — on a logarithmic horizontal scale for k = 20, 40, 60, 80, and 100 respectively in each subplot from left to right. The legend identifies seven methods: ACORN (lower bound), ACORN (upper bound), CAPS (kmeans), FDANN (filtered), FDANN (stitched), NHQ (igraph), NHQ (nsw), UNG — though only some appear plotted per chart, with colored markers and lines representing each method’s performance curve. The main trend across all charts is that higher recall values are achieved at lower QPS rates for most methods; as query throughput increases, accuracy typically drops sharply after a certain point, especially beyond 10^3–10^4 queries/sec depending on k. Some curves remain flat near Recall=1.0 up to high QPS (e.g., ACORN upper bound), while others decline steeply earlier or show intermediate behavior — suggesting trade-offs between speed and precision that vary by algorithm and selectivity level k.

This figure consists of seven line charts arranged side by side, each representing data from different Slimpajama dataset categories: Crawl, Exchange, C4, Github, Wikipedia, ArXiv, and Book. Each chart plots word length (from 1 to 10) on the x-axis against coverage percentage on the y-axis — though note that while Figure 9’s caption mentions “top n-length words,” these charts actually show cumulative or incremental coverage as more frequent short-word lengths are included up to a given max length. The headline above each chart displays both the dataset name and its total coverage achieved using all word lengths ≤10 (e.g., “Crawl 0.974” means 97.4% of words in that category have length ≤10). All lines start near or at full coverage for very short words (lengths 1–2) and gradually decline as longer maximum word lengths are considered — indicating diminishing returns from including rarer, longer words. The consistent high initial drop across all datasets confirms the caption’s claim: even with just top few most frequent word lengths, you cover over half; by length ≤5, coverage exceeds ~74%; and by length ≤10, it reaches ≥95% in every category shown.

This figure (Figure 5) from "ML-Embed: Inclusive and Efficient Embeddings for a Multilingual World" shows how different models perform as their embedding matrix rank increases during inference-time compression on MTEB-English tasks. The line chart plots three methods—Baseline, Decomposition-only, and MEL—with the x-axis showing ranks (100 to 1024) and y-axis measuring performance scores from ~30 to 70 points. Each method's curve uses distinct markers: circles for Baseline, diamonds for Decomposition-only, and squares for MEL—where all three start near identical low-rank performances but diverge significantly at higher ranks (e.g., rank 1024), with the green square-marked MEL line reaching ~69 points while others lag behind.

This figure is a pie chart showing how different models are distributed as evaluatees when using Gemma-2-2B as the evaluator. The center of the chart displays “gemma-2-2b-it” and notes that there were 1378 total instances evaluated around it — though this number appears inconsistent with the sum of percentages shown (which exceed 100%). Each slice represents a different model used for evaluation, labeled by name such as llama-3.1-dolphin-mistral-v2:9b or claude-3-haiku-20240307t568 — some with version tags like “v2” and others without clear scaling logic since multiple slices share identical percentage values (e.g., 1.7%, 1.9%) despite representing distinct models. The largest slice is labeled llama-3-dolphin-mistral-v4:0b at 6.5% of the total, while many smaller categories each account for less than 2%. No axis labels or legend are present — only model names and their proportional shares radiating outward from the center label indicating which evaluator was used (Gemma-2-2B) during these subjective task evaluations.

This figure contains six line charts arranged horizontally, each showing Recall@k versus Queries Per Second (QPS) for different values of k: 20, 40, 60, 80, and 100 — plus a sixth chart labeled “EMIS” at the top right. Each plot includes five methods plotted as lines with markers: ACORN (lower bound), ACORN (upper bound), FDANN (filtered), FDANN (stitched), and UNG; their legend is visible in each subplot. The x-axis on all plots ranges from 10¹ to 10³ QPS, while the y-axis shows Recall@k from 0.2 to 1.0. Across most subplots, ACORN methods maintain high recall near or above 0.9 even at higher query rates, whereas FDANN and UNG show steeper drops in performance as QPS increases — especially noticeable for k=80 and k=100 where some lines dip below 0.6 recall. The EMIS chart (top right) mirrors this pattern but appears to be an aggregate or comparative view rather than a specific k-value plot, since it lacks the “k=” label seen in others yet still displays identical method legends and axis scales.

This figure consists of three scatter plots arranged side by side, each representing performance data for different datasets: MuSiQue (left), FinanceBench (middle), and BrowseComp-Plus (right). The vertical axis on all charts is labeled “Accuracy,” ranging from 0.0 to above 0.5; the horizontal axis in each plot shows a logarithmic scale of cost per query, with values such as $10^{-4}$, $10^{-2}$, and up to $1$ USD for BrowseComp-Plus (note: “BrowseComP” appears mislabeled — likely meant to be “BrowseComp”). Each chart contains colored dots representing different methods or configurations—such as blue circles (“No Retrieval”), green squares (“Concatenate”), orange pentagons (“Agent Loop”)—and star-shaped markers indicating specific METIS variants paired with LLMs like GPT-5 nano, Gemini 3.1 Pro, etc., along their respective costs and accuracies. A dashed gray line labeled “Pareto frontier” traces the best achievable accuracy-cost trade-off across all tested configurations within each dataset’s plot. The overall structure reveals how various retrieval strategies perform relative to one another under different cost constraints, with some methods clustering near optimal frontiers while others fall behind or exceed them in efficiency versus effectiveness.

This figure illustrates an example of how perplexity (PPL) values are calculated for code generation tasks using large language models under two different conditions: with and without a review comment provided as input context. The table has three rows — the top row shows prompts (“Code Fix PPL with Review Comment” vs “without”), each containing system instructions, chat templates referencing LLaMA architecture examples, specific Go-style pseudocode snippets (e.g., `if opts.BeforeWrite != nil { ... }`), and a final line indicating whether to calculate perplexity. The middle row displays the actual code being evaluated in both cases — identical except that only one version includes an explicit review comment (“Should we perhaps disallow reading...”). The bottom right cell explicitly labels “Calculate Perplexity” under each condition, suggesting comparative evaluation of model output likelihoods based on contextual guidance. No axis or legend is present; it’s a structured textual example rather than a chart or diagram — clearly meant to demonstrate prompt design for training data construction in code review enhancement via LLM fine-tuning (as referenced by KTO algorithm mention nearby).

This figure consists of three scatter plots arranged side by side: MATH500 (left), MMLU (middle), and MBPP+ (right). Each plot shows “Self-Preference Ratio (%)” on the y-axis versus “Task Accuracy (%)” on the x-axis. Data points are colored to represent different LLM families — blue for Llana, green for Gemma, red/orange for Qwen — and sized by model scale: small (3B), moderate (7–9B), medium (14–32B), large (70–72B). A dashed diagonal line indicates perfect correlation; each plot includes a Pearson r value showing strong positive correlations: 0.801 for MATH500, 0.817 for MMLU, and 0.771 for MBPP+. The overall trend across all three plots is that higher task accuracy correlates with greater self-preference ratio — meaning models perform better at evaluating their own outputs when they are more accurate generators.

This figure is an architecture diagram comparing three different finetuning methods for large language models: Full Finetuning (No Adapters), LoRA, and QLoRa. It visually represents how each method handles memory usage through components like the Optimizer State (32 bit) stored in CPU RAM with paging flow shown by pink arrows; Adapter modules at 16-bit precision that receive gradient updates via green upward-pointing triangles indicating parameter update direction during backpropagation or forward pass depending on context — here likely representing weight adjustment paths from base model to adapters. The Base Model is depicted as a black rectangle containing multiple small rectangles symbolizing transformer layers, with blue downward arrows showing data flow into the 16-bit Transformer block beneath it in all three columns except QLoRa where only one such layer exists per column but connected via green bidirectional gradients and pink paging flows to external CPU storage. The main structure shows increasing efficiency: Full Finetuning uses full optimizer state without adapters, LoRA adds lightweight adapter layers while keeping 16-bit transformers intact, and QLoRa further reduces the base model’s precision down to a single “4-bit Transformer” block with dynamic memory management via paged optimizers — illustrated by curved pink arrows looping between CPU RAM blocks. No numerical values are explicitly labeled beyond bit-widths (32-bit optimizer state vs 16-bit adapters/transformer in first two columns, then just one unified transformer layer under QLoRa).

This figure consists of three horizontal bar charts arranged side by side, each showing "Target@3 uplift (pp)" on the x-axis ranging from 0 to approximately 75 pp. The y-axes list various prompt types grouped into four categories: Atomic (blue), Block (green), Cross-block (orange), and Realistic (red). Each chart corresponds to a different model — Devstral Small, Gemma 4 31B IT, Qwen3.6 27B Instruct/24B — as indicated in the caption above the figure. The bars represent performance uplift for each prompt type under that specific model; longer bars indicate higher uplift values. Across all three models, “Realistic” prompts consistently show high uplift (often near or exceeding 50 pp), while some Atomic and Block types vary more widely depending on the model — notably M-only shows very low uplift across all charts except possibly in one case where it’s slightly above zero but still minimal compared to others.

This figure consists of five side-by-side histograms showing the distribution of pairwise distances between sampled embedding vectors across different models: SIFT (image), Audio, UQ-V, Paper, and transformer-based (ours). Each histogram has “Frequency” on the y-axis and “Pairwise Distances between Sampled Vectors” on the x-axis. The green bars represent frequency counts for distance bins; scales vary significantly — e.g., UQ-V’s distances go up to 125 while others are under 70 or below 3, indicating vastly different magnitude ranges across modalities/models. All distributions appear right-skewed with peaks at higher values except SIFT and transformer-based which show bimodal-like shapes near their upper bounds. No legends beyond model names in titles; no gridlines or annotations other than axis labels and title bars above each plot.

This figure consists of six grouped bar charts arranged in two rows and three columns, comparing retrieval performance metrics across different model configurations for Llama3-8B (top row) and GPT-4 (bottom row). Each column represents a distinct evaluation metric: H@5 on the left, P@5 in the middle, and Acc on the right. The bars within each group correspond to five methods labeled at the top as “w/o GQR” (blue), “w/o KWR” (purple), “w/o PAR” (yellow), “w/o CCE” (orange-yellow), and “Ours” (salmon pink). Vertical dashed lines indicate baseline scores with their numerical values shown above them; bars show deviations from these baselines, annotated directly on the chart. The main trend shows that "Ours" consistently yields positive improvements over all other ablated versions across both models and metrics — for example, +1.7 in Acc for Llama3-8B under “Acc”, while others often fall below baseline (e.g., -0.90 or more negative).

This figure consists of four bar charts arranged in two rows and columns: 0-shot results on top left (top row), 2-shot results to its right; bottom-left shows another set for different tasks under same conditions as above but labeled differently ("mean", "hellaswag" etc.). Each chart displays accuracy scores across various benchmark datasets including mean, arc_challenge, piqa among others. The x-axis represents task names while y-axis indicates performance measured by 'acc' (accuracy). Two main methods compared are T-Free baseline and Unigram with varying parameters like 5k/10k tokens used during training phase denoted via color coding within each group of bars per dataset/task name combination shown along horizontal axis. Legend on far-right side clarifies which colors correspond to what methodological variations being tested out here visually represented through grouped vertical rectangular shapes whose heights reflect relative success rates achieved under given experimental setups described earlier textually above this visual representation itself!

This figure consists of three side-by-side bar charts comparing cost savings across different models and accuracy goals on datasets named MuSiQue, BrowseComp+, and FinanceBench. The vertical axis represents "Cost saving (%)" while the horizontal groups are labeled with specific targets like 100%, 95%, or 90% Acc Goal within each dataset section. A legend at the top identifies four models: GPT-5-mini (dark green), GPT-5-nano (light green), Qwen3.5-9B (purple), and text-embedding-3 (orange). The bars show that for high accuracy goals, some configurations like GPT-5-mini achieve significant cost savings over 80%, whereas lower targets often result in much smaller percentage gains or "n/a" hatched areas indicating unreachable costs.

This figure illustrates an architecture diagram detailing how Desiview4FT and Desiview4FA are developed through code review processes using large language models (LLMs). It shows components such as "Commit Co," "Review Comment R," "Fix Commit Cr" on the left side, indicating a common commit-review-fix cycle. In between steps involving LLMs generating scores for desiredness of comments and voting mechanisms to determine final Desiredness Scores are depicted in blue stars labeled Score 1 through Score 4'. On the right part there's Base LLM leading into Fine-tuning which produces Desiview4FT while Alignment leads towards creating another model named as 'DesiViewFA' with corresponding datasets shown below them. The main structure highlights how different elements interact within this process to enhance code reviews via AI-driven insights without explicitly stating any numerical trends but rather focusing on the flow and relationships between various stages of development involving LLMs at each step along side by their respective outputs like 'Desired Review Dataset' or Undesired ones based upon DS values greater than zero versus less equaling it respectively.

This figure is a stacked bar chart showing memory footprint breakdowns for different LLaMA model sizes: 7B (6.9 GB), 13B (11.3 GB), 33B (24.7 GB), and 65B (45.0 GB). Each vertical bar represents total GPU memory usage, segmented by component type — shown in the legend as Input gradient (orange), Optimizer (green), Weight gradient (yellow), Adapters (red), and Model weights (blue) — with numerical values labeled on each segment indicating MB consumed per part of that model. The y-axis ranges from 0% to over 100%, suggesting relative scaling or normalization across models, though absolute memory usage increases significantly as model size grows: for example, the “Model” component alone rises from ~5 GB in LLaMA-7B to nearly 38 GB in LLaMA-65B. The chart visually demonstrates how larger models demand substantially more VRAM, especially due to their base weights and optimizer states — with QLoRA’s adapters consuming relatively little memory even at scale (e.g., only ~140 MB for the largest model).

This figure contains multiple subplots (labeled **a** through **h**) that combine architecture diagrams and data visualizations to illustrate how pretraining with random noise affects neural network confidence across different input spaces — from 2D toy models to high-dimensional image inputs. In subplot **(b)**, two scatter plots show “Confidence” mapped over Feature 1 vs. Feature 2: the left plot (“Untrained”) displays a gradient of red-to-blue indicating varying confidence levels, while the right plot (“Randomly pretrained”) shows uniformly blue dots near low confidence (~0.5), suggesting calibration toward chance level; color bars indicate confidence ranges (left: ~0–1, right: ~0.48–0.6). Subplots **(c)** and**(d)** are box plots comparing “Confidence bias” and“Std of class ratio” between untrained vs randomly pretrained networks for the 2D case — both show statistically significant differences marked by asterisks (*), with random pretraining reducing confidence variance closer to chance (0.5). Similarly, subplots **(f)**,**(g)**,**(h) extend this analysis to a high-dimension model using 32x32x3 images and 10-class labels: subplot(f)’s scatter plots show softmax probabilities per readout index — untrained outputs vary widely above chance (dashed line at ~0.5), while randomly pretrained ones cluster tightly around it;**(g)** confirms reduced confidence bias, and **(h) shows lower standard deviation of class ratios after random pretraining.** The overall structure demonstrates that training on arbitrary noise with BCE loss calibrates network uncertainty across architectures — pushing predictions toward uniform randomness rather than overconfident or biased outputs.

This figure contains four panels (a–d) that together illustrate how out-of-distribution detection works using calibrated network confidence from pretraining with random noise. Panel a shows conceptual diagrams of ID classes (“ID Class 0” and “ID Class 1”) as clustered blue/orange dots, alongside gray OOD points representing unseen data like digits or animals not in the training set — labeled CIFAR-10 for ID and SVHN for OOD. Panels b and d include histograms/boxplots (b) showing confidence distributions (“w/o” vs “w/ random pretraining”) where w/ has lower median confidence on unknowns, marked with an asterisk indicating statistical significance; panel d’s ROC curve compares true positive rate against false positive rate between models trained without (orange line) and with (blue line) random noise — the blue curve dominates. The boxplots in b and d both show AUROC performance: “w/” achieves higher median (~0.85 vs ~0.72), again marked significant (*). All panels use color coding consistently: orange for baseline (“w/o”), blue for improved method (“w/”).

This figure consists of three scatter plots arranged horizontally under the title "Subjective Tasks from LMArena." Each plot has Task Accuracy (%) on its x-axis and a different metric on its y-axis: Judge Accuracy (%), Self-Preference Ratio (%), or Legitimate Self-Preference Ratio (%). The data points represent five large language models—Llama, Gemma, Qwen—at varying parameter sizes (Small 2B to Large 70–72B), indicated by color and size in the legend. All three plots show a positive correlation between task accuracy and their respective y-axis metrics, with Pearson’s r values displayed as $r = 0.730$, $r = 0.649$, and $r = 0.959$. The trend lines slope upward across all subplots, indicating that higher model performance correlates strongly with increased self-preference or judge accuracy in subjective tasks.

This figure illustrates an evaluation process for code review using large language models and distilled datasets. It includes components like "Sampled dataset," "Manual annotation," "Annotated dataset," "Various data distillation methods" (including Desview4FT and Desview4FA), and two types of results: automated via a gear icon, human via an avatar with checkmark or cross icons for judgment evaluation. The structure shows parallel pathways — one leading to manual annotations feeding into result analysis; another showing fine-tuning datasets being processed through distillation methods toward both automated and human evaluations. Arrows indicate flow from sampling → annotation/distillation → results across two main boxes labeled by research question focus: desiredness judgement (top) vs improvement-based evaluation (bottom). No axis labels or legends are present — it’s a conceptual architecture diagram, not quantitative data visualization.

This figure is a confusion matrix comparing LLM sufficiency judgments against human majority votes for evidence adequacy. The vertical axis (LLM) and horizontal axis (Human Majority) each have two categories: “Not Suff” and “Sufficient.” Four cells display counts of agreement or disagreement between the models, with darker shading indicating higher values — notably 92 in the bottom-right cell where both LLM and humans judged evidence as sufficient. The top-left cell shows 28 cases where neither deemed it sufficient; other off-diagonal cells show mismatches (e.g., 21 when human said “Sufficient” but LLM did not). This structure reveals strong agreement on sufficiency judgments, especially in the positive case, with fewer disagreements elsewhere.

The figure appears to be an example of text rather than any kind of chart or diagram such as architecture diagrams, line charts, bar charts, tables images, screenshots etc., it shows a table with two columns labeled "Evaluator Prompt (CoT)" and the content under this column is not readable in detail but seems like some instructions for evaluating answers using Chain-of-Thought reasoning.

This figure illustrates two methods for encoding and decoding text: classic tokenization (left) versus T-FREE’s sparse representation approach (right). The top half shows how “Hello_word!” — broken into trigrams like [H,e,l], [e,ll,o] etc., or hashed characters such as {He, el, lo} in the right panel — is mapped to embeddings via lookup tables; both use an embedding dimension labeled ‘h’. In decoding (bottom), classic tokenization uses a single-class vocabulary where each word maps uniquely to one bar height on its probability distribution curve. T-FREE’s multi-class vocabularies show overlapping activations across multiple bars per input, reflecting shared morphological features among words like “mouse,” “house,” and “ouse.” The structure emphasizes that while both encode/decode text through embeddings with dimension h, only the right-side method leverages sparse overlaps to compress representations.

This figure is an architecture diagram illustrating how simulated opinions are generated using large language models (LLMs) with derived roles. It shows a central input prompt that creates two distinct “Created Roles”: Conservative-Leaning and Liberal-Leaning, each defined by specific agreeableness traits — the former values firm stances and less consensus-seeking behavior, while the latter prioritizes cooperation and compromise. Both role descriptions feed into an LLM component represented as a green square with icons of gears and people symbolizing processing or simulation logic. The output flows downward to produce “Simulated Opinion,” indicating that opposing viewpoints can be modeled through tailored persona inputs rather than relying on real-world data alone — suggesting this method enables controlled exploration of public opinion dynamics in digital democracy contexts like eDemocracy platforms mentioned elsewhere (though not visible here).

This figure consists of seven subplots (a–g) that combine schematic diagrams and data visualizations to illustrate how pretraining with random noise improves confidence calibration in neural networks. Subplot a shows spontaneous brain activity before sensory input; b maps developmental timelines for vision/hearing systems; c depicts the algorithm using Gaussian-distributed inputs paired uniformly across labels — all inspired by prenatal learning (d) compares test loss curves: blue line (“w/ pretraining”) drops faster than red (“o/w”), indicating quicker convergence. Inset accuracy plot confirms higher final performance with pretraining over 30 epochs.

Subplots e–g quantify calibration improvements via histograms, reliability diagrams showing reduced Expected Calibration Error (ECE), and heatmaps where deeper networks benefit more from pretraining — especially at larger training sizes. All axes are labeled clearly: time in ms or days post-birth; pixel intensity range ±4σ; epoch count up to 30/15+epochs; confidence vs accuracy ranges [0,1]; ECE scaled ×10³ on colorbar (blue=low error). The overall structure demonstrates that pretraining mimics biological development and yields better-calibrated predictions without sacrificing generalization.
